title: AI, chips and India: on both sides of the biggest spending boom in decades
hook:
On a Monday in January 2025, Nvidia, the company whose chips power almost every serious AI model, lost close to six hundred billion dollars of market value in a single session, the largest one-day wipeout for any stock in Wall Street history. The trigger was a little-known Chinese start-up called DeepSeek, which had released a free AI assistant it claimed was built for a fraction of what American labs spend. If clever software could do more with fewer chips, investors asked, what happens to the trillion-dollar bet on chips?

Here's the curious part. Indian IT stocks, companies that make no chips and train no models, fell too, and kept sliding for weeks. Why would a Chinese chatbot hurt software houses in Bengaluru and Pune?

Because the AI boom reaches India from two directions at once. It is a customer for Indian factories, power equipment and data centres. And it is a threat to the business model that made Indian IT famous. This chapter follows the money from American cloud giants through Korean memory chips and Taiwanese foundries to Indian stocks, and explains why you should never treat India's AI exposure as one trade.
short: The AI build-out is the largest corporate investment cycle since the telecom boom of the late 1990s, and a growing share of it is funded with debt.
Korea's monthly exports are the earliest hard reading of AI demand, because Korea makes most of the world's high-bandwidth memory, the chips that feed AI processors.
Chips are now weapons: US export controls decide which chips China can buy, and China's controls on rare earths decide what the rest of the world can build.
India gains from the build-out through electronics, power equipment, data centres and its first chip plants, but AI coding tools press on the billable hours Indian IT lives on.
An AI credit wobble would hit both sides of India's exposure through foreign flows, so keep the two trades apart and watch the funding, not just the hype.

sections.heading: The biggest spending spree since the telecom boom
sections.html:
Start with the money. A handful of American companies, the hyperscalers, which is the industry's word for the giant cloud providers that rent computing to everyone else, are spending at a pace the corporate world has rarely seen. Estimates for this year run to several hundred billion dollars, for chips, memory, servers, buildings and the power to run them. For the biggest spenders, capital spending now rivals the cash their businesses throw off.

So where does the rest come from? Increasingly, from borrowing. By one recent estimate about a third of AI capital spending is now funded with debt: bonds from the big platforms, loans to specialist AI cloud companies, and project finance tied to individual data centres.

Why should you care how it is paid for? Because it changes who gets hurt if the payoff is late. When a company spends its own cash and the bet disappoints, shareholders lose. When it borrows, lenders are exposed too, and lenders have lenders. Stress travels.

When a boom runs on borrowed money, the question is not whether the technology works, but whether the cash arrives before the interest falls due.

The first cracks have appeared at the weak end. Some specialist AI cloud providers, younger firms that borrowed heavily to buy chips and rent them out, have seen their bonds trade at distressed yields, and banks have started to limit how much AI debt they will hold. The big platforms remain solidly investment grade.

For India the link is indirect but real. The flood of AI-related bonds adds to the supply pressure behind high US Treasury yields, and high US yields pull money out of emerging markets. And if an AI credit event rattled Wall Street, global investors would cut risk everywhere, and Indian shares, liquid and widely owned, are always among the first things sold.

sections.heading: Follow the chip: who makes what, and where India fits
sections.html:
An AI model looks like pure software, but underneath it sits one of the most concentrated supply chains on earth. A few American firms design the processors. Almost all leading-edge logic chips are manufactured in Taiwan, mostly by one company, TSMC. The memory stacked beside those processors comes mostly from two Korean companies, SK Hynix and Samsung. The machines that print the smallest circuits come from a single Dutch firm, ASML. Every layer is a chokepoint.

[[fig:1]]

Read the diagram top to bottom on the left: money starts with the model makers and cloud giants, flows down into chip design, then into foundries and memory makers, then into the servers and networking gear that hold the chips, and finally into the land, grid connections and cooling that data centres need. The right-hand column shows India's position at each layer. The top box stands apart because it is the one layer where AI is a threat as much as an opportunity for India: it is where the IT services industry sits. Every box below it is a potential order book.

Notice where India is strongest. Not at the glamorous top, but at the two ends. Bengaluru and Hyderabad host the design centres of nearly every big chip company in the world, where Indian engineers design and verify chips they never get to manufacture. And at the bottom, the build-out is a physical business: transformers, switchgear, transmission lines, cables, backup power, server assembly. Those are things Indian manufacturers already make and are now selling to data-centre builders at home and abroad. The middle layers, actually making chips, are where India is only beginning.

sections.heading: Why Korea's export numbers are the AI boom's pulse
sections.html:
If you want to know how strong AI demand is right now, don't wait for American earnings calls. Look at Korea. Korea publishes its trade figures on the first day of every month, with early readings even before the month ends. Semiconductors are its biggest export. So Korea's numbers are the fastest hard data on the planet about chip demand.

The key product is high-bandwidth memory, or HBM. An AI processor is a ferociously fast calculator, but it is useless if data cannot reach it fast enough; engineers call this the memory wall. HBM solves it by stacking memory chips on top of one another like floors of a building, wiring them vertically, and placing the stack right next to the processor. It is hard to make and hard to package. SK Hynix is the leading supplier and Nvidia's main source, with Samsung and America's Micron behind.

That is why Korea's September 2026 numbers turned heads. Total exports hit a record, and chip exports more than tripled from a year earlier, making up roughly half of everything the country sold abroad. Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan said Korea was on course to pass a trillion dollars of exports in a year for the first time, while flagging protectionism and Middle East tensions as risks.

Here's the catch. Memory is the most cyclical corner of the chip industry. Supply arrives in giant lumps, because a new factory takes years to build and then floods the market, while demand swings with every change in mood. When prices rise, everyone expands; by the time the new capacity arrives, the shortage is over. So read Korea's data two ways: for momentum, and for the turn. The moment to worry is not when growth is strong, but when it starts to slow while capacity is still coming on.

sections.heading: Chips as weapons
sections.html:
In October 2022 the US Commerce Department drew a line: no more of the most advanced AI chips, or the tools to make them, for China. Nvidia responded by designing slowed-down versions that fell just under the limits, Washington tightened the rules again, and the cat-and-mouse has continued ever since. The Netherlands and Japan were persuaded to restrict their chipmaking machines too.

China answered with its own lever: the minerals. It restricted exports of gallium and germanium, metals used in chips, in 2023, and in April 2025 put strict licensing on rare earths and the magnets made from them, which sit inside every electric motor from a scooter to a fighter jet. The pain reached India quickly. By May 2025, Rakesh Sharma of Bajaj Auto was warning that India's vehicle output could take a hit as early as July if magnet shipments did not resume.

The lesson is that both sides now treat technology as a bargaining chip, permanently. Export controls decide which chips China can buy; Chinese mineral controls decide what everyone else can build.

For India this cuts both ways. Companies that want to reduce their dependence on China, the China-plus-one strategy, are looking at India for electronics assembly, components and even chip packaging, which is a genuine tailwind for Indian manufacturers. But India also depends on China for many of the inputs those factories use. A friend of both camps gets orders from both, and pressure from both.

sections.heading: India's chip dream, take two
sections.html:
India has been here before, as the history below tells. This time the approach is different. In December 2021 the government launched the India Semiconductor Mission, offering to pay roughly half the cost of approved chip projects. The first attempt to use it, a Vedanta and Foxconn fab, collapsed in 2023 when Foxconn walked out. Then the projects started to stick.

To see why the order matters, split chipmaking in two. The front end, the fab, prints circuits onto silicon wafers. It needs billions of dollars, ultra-pure water, power that never flickers and years of painful learning before most chips come out working. The back end, called assembly and test, cuts the wafers into chips, packages them and checks them. It costs far less and suits a country that is good at precise, large-scale manufacturing.

India sensibly started at the back. Micron, the American memory maker, announced an assembly and test plant at Sanand in Gujarat in 2023; it was inaugurated in early 2026 and is shipping. Other packaging plants are following. The first real fab, a Tata Electronics venture with Taiwan's Powerchip at Dholera, is under construction, with first output expected somewhere between late 2026 and 2028 depending on whom you ask.

And packaging is no consolation prize. HBM's whole trick is packaging: stacking chips and sitting them beside the processor. Advanced packaging has become one of the tightest bottlenecks in AI hardware.

For the stock market, the semiconductor mission shows up less in pure chip stocks, which are few, and more in electronics manufacturing services companies, component makers, industrial gas and chemical suppliers, and the power and construction firms building the plants.

sections.heading: Why Indian IT feels the AI boom as a headwind
sections.html:
Now the uncomfortable side. Indian IT services grew rich on a simple model: clients pay for people's time. A big project means hundreds of engineers writing, testing and maintaining code, billed by the hour or by the person, arranged in a pyramid with many juniors at the bottom.

AI coding tools attack the base of that pyramid. If a tool writes the first draft of the code, generates the tests and documents the old system, the client needs fewer hours. And clients know it: at contract renewal they ask for the productivity gain to be passed on as a lower price. Meanwhile, technology budgets that might have gone to large outsourcing deals are being redirected to AI infrastructure. And more multinationals run their own captive offices in India, called global capability centres, doing work they once outsourced.

There is an upside. Somebody has to connect AI to a bank's thirty-year-old systems, clean the data, and run it securely, and Indian firms are well placed. But so far the hours lost have been easier to see than the hours gained, and the largest firms have reported muted demand.

[[fig:2]]

The chart shows three panels, each starting at a hundred in August 2023. The top, green, is an illustrative basket of Indian companies building the AI economy's plumbing: an AI-server maker, power equipment and transmission firms and electronics manufacturers. It has climbed far ahead. The middle, red, is four of the biggest IT services firms: up for a while, then rolling over, and now below where it started. The marker shows DeepSeek. The bottom panel is the Nifty, for scale. Same boom, two opposite outcomes.

history_title: booms, busts and the chips in between

history.title: The night India's chip dream burned
history.story:
In the 1980s India had a real chip factory. Semiconductor Complex Limited in Mohali, Punjab, began production in the mid-1980s and, by some accounts, was not far behind the global leaders of its day. Then, late on a February night in 1989, fire broke out. It started at several points at once, burned until morning and gutted the fabrication and research areas. Nobody died, but the plant was wrecked.

Sabotage was suspected; the Intelligence Bureau investigated and the inquiry came back inconclusive. Rebuilding took years, and the world did not wait. Taiwan's TSMC, founded only a couple of years earlier, went on to become the most important factory on earth. India spent the next three decades designing chips for others.
history.lesson: In chips, a lost decade is permanent: the industry compounds, and late entrants pay for every year missed.

history.title: The millennium bug and the bell at Nasdaq
history.story:
In the late 1990s the world panicked that old computer programs, which stored years using only their last two figures, would read the year 2000 as 1900 and crash banks and airlines at midnight. Fixing millions of lines of ancient code was tedious work, and Indian programmers did it well and cheaply. In March 1999 Infosys, the Bengaluru firm co-founded by N. R. Narayana Murthy, became the first Indian company listed on Nasdaq.

Indian IT stocks rocketed with the dot-com boom, then crashed with it in 2000 and 2001. But the millennium-bug work had got Indian firms through the door of every big Western company, and they stayed to run the systems they had fixed.
history.lesson: Technology booms overbuild and bust, but the firms that turn a fad into a durable service survive the crash.

history.title: The fibre glut that built Bengaluru's back offices
history.story:
During the dot-com boom, telecom companies borrowed heavily to lay fibre-optic cables across oceans and continents, betting internet traffic would grow forever. It grew, just not fast enough. Global Crossing filed for bankruptcy in early 2002 and WorldCom collapsed that summer amid an accounting fraud. Much of the fibre sat unused, and lenders took the losses.

The twist: that glut made it almost free to send data between America and India. Thomas Friedman opened his book The World Is Flat with Nandan Nilekani of Infosys telling him the global playing field was being levelled. The overbuilt cables carried Bengaluru's call centres, back offices and software work to the world.
history.lesson: Debt-funded infrastructure booms end in write-offs even when the technology wins, and someone else gets the cheap capacity.

history.title: The year memory dethroned Intel
history.story:
In 2017 a shortage sent memory chip prices soaring, and Samsung overtook Intel as the world's largest chipmaker by revenue, ending a reign Intel had held since the early 1990s. Korea's exports boomed and analysts spoke of a supercycle, the idea that demand from smartphones and data centres had broken the old boom-and-bust pattern.

It had not. New factories came on, demand cooled, and memory prices tumbled through 2018 and 2019. Korea's chip exports fell sharply and Samsung lost the crown back to Intel.
history.lesson: Memory is the most cyclical part of the chip chain, and Korea's data turns first; whenever someone says supercycle, check the capacity pipeline.

history.title: When India's carmakers ran out of chips
history.story:
When the pandemic hit, carmakers cancelled chip orders, expecting a long slump. Instead, people stuck at home bought laptops and, soon, cars. Chipmakers had given the car industry's slots to electronics firms, and a modern car needs a great many chips. In September 2021 Maruti Suzuki, India's biggest carmaker, warned that output at its plants would fall to well under half of normal because of a shortage of electronic components.

Showrooms emptied, waiting lists for popular models stretched for months, and the festive season, normally the year's best, was a washout for car sales.
history.lesson: Supply-chain concentration can turn into a production crisis overnight, even for companies that never thought of themselves as chip buyers.

history.title: Two shocks from America
history.story:
In October 2022 Washington imposed sweeping limits on advanced chips and chipmaking tools for China, turning technology into an instrument of geopolitics. Weeks later, in November, OpenAI released ChatGPT, and within months every board in the world was asking for an AI strategy.

In May 2023 Nvidia, run by its leather-jacketed co-founder Jensen Huang, told investors its next quarter's revenue would be far above anything analysts had imagined. Its stock leapt and the company's value soon passed a trillion dollars. The market had found the purest picks-and-shovels play of the gold rush.
history.lesson: The market rewards the picks-and-shovels first; the companies that must prove AI earns them money are judged later and harder.

today:
The boom and its funding risk are rising together. Korea's September exports were a record, led by chips. At the same time, US cloud spending is increasingly debt-funded, and banks are pulling back from holding more of that debt. The latest readings, checked on the web, are below.

[[fig:3]]

Read the box as a dashboard with two halves. The top rows are demand: Korean exports and cloud capital spending, both at or near records. The middle row is the funding: a third of the spending on borrowed money. The last two rows are India's own chip story: one plant shipping, one fab still being built.

For Indian markets, the AI trade is also a rates trade. The US ten-year Treasury yield is [[val:us10y]], and foreign investors have sold [[val:fii20]] of Indian shares over the past twenty sessions. On the latest trading day, Nifty IT jumped on easing fears about AI disruption, its most unusual move of the session. One good day does not remove a structural headwind.

What to watch next: Korea's trade data on the first of each month; the quarterly capital-spending guidance of the big US cloud companies; memory contract prices; credit spreads on AI-linked debt; and progress at Dholera.
sowhat:
Keep India's two AI trades apart, and watch the funding as closely as the demand.

  • Prefer the build-out: power equipment and transmission, electronics manufacturing services, data-centre operators and AI-server makers. It has the momentum and the order books, though valuations already assume a lot.
  • Be careful with IT services. The disruption to billable hours is structural, and a single strong day does not remove it. Firms that show real AI-led revenue growth, not just AI announcements, are the exception to look for.
  • Watch Korean export growth and memory prices as the early warning. When growth slows while new capacity is still arriving, the cycle is turning.
  • Remember an AI credit event would hit both sides through foreign selling, whatever the fundamentals.

What would flip it: US cloud giants cutting their spending guidance, Korean chip exports rolling over, or AI credit spreads blowing out would all hurt the build-out trade. Clear evidence that AI is creating more paid work for Indian IT than it destroys would re-rate the other side.
